stem: In his surrender message, what reason does Chief Joseph give for stopping the fight?

stimulus.source_note: Chief Joseph's surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877, as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood, aide to General Howard; printed in Harper's Weekly, November 17, 1877. Public domain. Text verified against the University of Washington Libraries transcription of Harper's Weekly and the National Park Service account of the Nez Perce surrender.
stimulus.text:
Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, surrender message, Bear Paw Mountains, Montana Territory, October 1877 (as transcribed by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood; ellipses mark omissions):

"Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before I have in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Tu-hul-hul-sote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led the young men is dead. It is cold and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food. No one knows where they are - perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children, and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

options.text: His people had reached Canada and safety
options.misconception: Background: the Nez Perce were stopped short of Canada in the Bear Paw Mountains; they never reached safety.

options.text: General Howard had promised to return the Wallowa Valley to the Nez Perce
options.misconception: Background: Howard demanded the move to an Idaho reservation; no promise to return the Wallowa homeland appears in the message.

options.text: His chiefs were dead, his children were freezing, and his people were scattered
His warriors had decided to join the Lakota at Little Bighorn
options.misconception: Background: Little Bighorn was fought in 1876, a year earlier, by Lakota and Cheyenne, not the Nez Perce.

rationales.A: Background: the Nez Perce were stopped short of Canada in the Bear Paw Mountains. They never reached safety.
rationales.B: Background: Howard demanded the move to an Idaho reservation. No promise to return the Wallowa homeland appears in the message.
rationales.C: Joseph names the dead chiefs, the freezing children, and the scattered people. He surrenders because his people can no longer survive the flight, not because they have won.
rationales.D: Background: Little Bighorn was fought in 1876, a year earlier, by Lakota and Cheyenne, not the Nez Perce.
rationales.general:
Picture a cold mountain camp in October, with soldiers closing in and children freezing.
1. Listen for what Joseph counts. Dead chiefs, dead old men, a dead leader of the young men.
2. Listen for what his people lack. No blankets, no food, children freezing, families scattered in the hills.
3. Name his reason. He stops because his people cannot go on, not because he has changed his mind.
Remember: a surrender can be a count of losses, not a change of heart.
